question: What is the OWASP Mobile Top 10 and what should every mobile dev know about it?
answer:
The OWASP Mobile Top 10 names the ten risk categories that most often break real mobile apps, and the 2024 revision is the current one.

• M1 Improper Credential Usage — hardcoded API keys, secrets committed to source.
• M2 Inadequate Supply Chain Security — vulnerable or over-privileged third-party SDKs.
• M3 Insecure Authentication / Authorization — weak token storage, authorization decided on the client.
• M4 Insufficient Input/Output Validation — injection, and XSS inside WebViews.
• M5 Insecure Communication — missing TLS, weak ciphers, no pinning.
• M6 Inadequate Privacy Controls — collecting more PII than declared, no consent gate.
• M7 Insufficient Binary Protections — no obfuscation or integrity checks where the threat model needs them.
• M8 Security Misconfiguration — debug endpoints in production, components left exported.
• M9 Insecure Data Storage — secrets in plain SharedPreferences or UserDefaults. Note that Jetpack Security's `EncryptedSharedPreferences` is deprecated, so new Android code should encrypt with a Keystore-held key itself rather than reaching for that library.
• M10 Insufficient Cryptography — broken algorithms, home-grown constructions, reused nonces.

How to use it: treat it as a review checklist rather than trivia. Thread the categories through code review, run static analysis (MobSF, Detekt security rules, AppSweep), scan dependencies on every bump, and buy a penetration test for anything handling money or health data.

The interview version of this question is usually 'which of these have you actually hit' — having a concrete story about one beats reciting all ten.

question: What does it take to make mobile API traffic hard to intercept and hard to replay?
answer:
No single control protects mobile API traffic, so you layer transport security, token hygiene and server-side attestation on the assumption that every client-side control will eventually be patched out.

• TLS, non-negotiable. Disable cleartext on Android and ship no ATS exceptions on iOS; require TLS 1.2 or better and reject anything older.
• Certificate or SPKI pinning defeats a rogue or user-installed CA. Pin the SPKI hash rather than the leaf certificate, always ship a backup pin, and rotate before expiry — a pinning mistake bricks every installed copy at once and cannot be hotfixed.
• OAuth 2.0 or OIDC with PKCE, in a system browser tab. Never an embedded WebView, never a hand-rolled flow.
• Short-lived access tokens measured in minutes, refresh tokens in Keychain or Keystore, and refresh-token rotation so a stolen one becomes detectable.
• Device and app attestation — Play Integrity on Android, App Attest or DeviceCheck on iOS. It only means something when your server validates the token; a client-side check of the verdict is theatre. Play Integrity's standard request, where you prepare a token provider once and then request per call, is the one to use for anything called often; classic requests are slow and rate-limited.
• Replay protection on endpoints that move money or change credentials: a server-issued nonce plus request signing, with a short validity window.
• Rate limiting and anomaly detection server-side, because that is the one layer an attacker cannot patch.

Say the quiet part out loud in an interview: pinning and obfuscation raise the attacker's cost, they do not stop one. Anything you must genuinely enforce belongs on the server.

question: Client-side root and jailbreak checks can be hooked out in minutes. What do you rely on instead, and what is a client-side check still worth?
answer:
Treat the client's answer as a signal and the server's attestation verdict as the decision — a rooted device can lie about being rooted, so anything enforced only on the client is enforced nowhere.

Server-side attestation, which is what actually holds:
• Play Integrity (Android) returns device labels — `MEETS_BASIC_INTEGRITY`, `MEETS_DEVICE_INTEGRITY`, `MEETS_STRONG_INTEGRITY` for hardware-backed evaluation, and `MEETS_VIRTUAL_INTEGRITY` for emulators — plus separate app and account verdicts. Your backend validates the token and maps the labels to a trust level.
• App Attest and DeviceCheck (iOS) prove the request came from a genuine, unmodified build of your app on real hardware, with a Secure Enclave key bound to that install.

Client-side heuristics, worth having only as an extra signal:
• Android — an `su` binary on the path, BusyBox, Magisk artefacts, test-keys in the build fingerprint, `ro.debuggable` set in a release build. RootBeer bundles the usual set; Magisk's hiding modules defeat most of them.
• iOS — Cydia and apt paths present, writes succeeding outside the sandbox, a registered `cydia` URL scheme handler, unexpected dynamic libraries in the process. IOSSecuritySuite bundles these.
• Both — a debugger attached, or Frida and Objection hooks visible in the process.

On a cross-platform runtime the probe is never yours to make directly:
• Dart, JavaScript and Kotlin/Native see none of these signals — every check is native code reached through a plugin or a channel, so a plugin-free app cannot answer the question at all.
• The resulting boolean lands in a Dart snapshot or a JS bundle, which is cheaper to patch than native code. Ship obfuscated and re-decide server-side.
• Build-mode flags (`kDebugMode`, `__DEV__`) describe your build, not the device, and are not a root check.

What to do with the answer:
• Do not hard-block. Custom ROMs and developer devices are common false positives, and a hard block is the first thing an attacker patches out anyway.
• Degrade by risk instead: refuse to enrol biometrics, force step-up authentication, decline high-value payments, shorten session lifetime.
• Make the decision server-side and send it back as policy the client applies, so the branch an attacker wants to flip is not sitting in the binary.
• Do not name detection functions descriptively and do not tell the user which check fired — that is writing the attacker's changelog for them.

question: Where does a private key actually live on Android and iOS, and how do you guarantee it cannot be extracted?
answer:
The answer to 'where do I put the private key' is 'somewhere you cannot read it either' — both platforms generate the key inside hardware and only ever let you ask it to sign or decrypt.

Android, through the `AndroidKeyStore` provider:
• Generate with `KeyGenParameterSpec`; the key material never enters your process memory.
• StrongBox puts the key in a separate secure element, but throws when the device has no StrongBox, so always catch that and fall back to the TEE-backed key rather than crashing on cheap hardware.
• `setUserAuthenticationRequired(true)` gates use behind biometrics or the device credential, combined with `BiometricPrompt` and a `CryptoObject`.
• `setAttestationChallenge(...)` yields a certificate chain your server can verify. That is what turns 'I promise this key is hardware-backed' into something checkable.
• Enrolling a new biometric invalidates the key if you asked for that — treat the resulting exception as a re-enrolment trigger, not a crash.

iOS, through the Secure Enclave:
• P-256 keys only, for signing and key agreement. CryptoKit's `SecureEnclave.P256.Signing.PrivateKey` is the readable API; the Keychain equivalent sets `kSecAttrTokenID` to `kSecAttrTokenIDSecureEnclave`.
• `SecAccessControl` binds usage to `.biometryCurrentSet`, which invalidates when Face ID or Touch ID enrolment changes, or to `.userPresence` when you want the passcode to be an acceptable fallback.
• Pick the accessibility class deliberately — the `ThisDeviceOnly` variants stop an item riding a backup onto a different device.

Cross-cutting:
• AES-GCM for symmetric, ECDSA or Ed25519 for signatures, ECDH for agreement, HKDF for derivation. RSA only when a peer forces it, and never a construction of your own design.
• Never reuse a GCM nonce under the same key; store the IV next to the ciphertext.
• Design for rotation on day one: the server accepts several public keys per user during the overlap window, and you re-key on reinstall, on biometric change, and on a failed attestation.

question: How do you keep sensitive content out of screenshots, screen recordings and the clipboard?
answer:
You cannot stop someone photographing the screen, so the goal is narrower: keep secrets out of screenshots, out of the recents thumbnail, out of screen recordings, and out of a clipboard other apps can read.

Screenshots and recording:
• Android — `FLAG_SECURE` on the window blocks screenshots, blanks the surface in recordings, and hides the recents thumbnail. It is per-window, so dialogs and separately presented surfaces need it too.
• Android 14 added a screen-capture callback so you can react to a screenshot instead of only blocking it, and Android 15 added a way to hide just the recents thumbnail without the full `FLAG_SECURE` blackout.
• iOS has no equivalent of `FLAG_SECURE`. You observe the user-took-a-screenshot notification after the fact, watch `UIScreen.isCaptured` while a recording is running, and cover the window with a placeholder as the scene resigns active so the app-switcher snapshot shows nothing.

Clipboard:
• Do not auto-copy secrets. If a one-time code really must be copied, clear it on a timer.
• Android 13 and later — mark the clip with the sensitive-content flag so the system's clipboard preview does not render the value, and the OS clears the clipboard itself after a period. Android also toasts when another app reads the clipboard, so assume every read is observable.
• iOS — set an `expirationDate` on the pasteboard item, and keep it local to the device so it does not travel over Universal Clipboard.

Keyboard and text fields:
• Use the platform's secure input — `SecureTextField` in Compose, `isSecureTextEntry` in UIKit, `SecureField` in SwiftUI. It also excludes the field from recordings.
• Turn off suggestion learning on sensitive fields so secrets never enter the keyboard's personal dictionary.

question: Before an app can ship, what privacy declarations and consent gates does each store require?
answer:
Privacy is a shipping gate now rather than a policy document — both stores reject builds whose declarations do not match what the binary actually does.

Apple:
• App Tracking Transparency — request authorization before any SDK that tracks the user across apps or sites runs, and read the advertising identifier only when the status is authorized. Initialising an ad SDK before the prompt is a rejection, not a warning.
• Privacy nutrition labels in App Store Connect — which data types you collect and whether they are linked to identity.
• Privacy manifests (`PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy`), required since 2024. Declare tracking domains and an approved reason code for each required-reason API you touch, such as user defaults, file timestamps, or disk space. Third-party SDKs on Apple's list must ship their own manifest and a code signature, so an SDK that has not caught up becomes your submission problem.

Google:
• The Data safety form in Play Console — collected, shared, retained, encrypted in transit, deletable.
• The advertising ID needs its permission declared, and it vanishes when the user opts out, so never treat it as a stable identifier.
• Apps with accounts need an in-app account deletion path and a web deletion URL.

GDPR and its relatives:
• Establish a lawful basis, and gate non-essential SDK initialisation on consent. The SDK must not start before the user answers, which means the gate belongs in the startup path, not in a screen.
• Build the user-rights endpoints for real: access, export, deletion. Deletion has to reach the device too — local database, caches, Keychain and Keystore entries.
• Watch data residency for EU and UK users; some contracts require the data never to leave the region.

Engineering practice: keep an inventory of every SDK and what it sends on first launch, and re-audit on every version bump. An SDK update is an unreviewed change to your privacy posture.

question: Your app unlocks itself when the biometric API returns true. What is wrong with that, and what does a correct flow look like?
answer:
A biometric API that returns a boolean proves nothing, because whoever can patch the app can patch the boolean. A correct flow makes the biometric unlock a key, so the successful decryption is the proof and there is no branch to flip.

What biometrics actually are:
• A local gate over a credential you already hold, not an authentication factor your server ever sees. The face or fingerprint never leaves the device and never reaches your backend; what it does is decide whether this client may use its stored token.
• So the thing you protect is the token or key, and the design question is always what the biometric unlocks.

Android:
• `BiometricPrompt` with a `CryptoObject`. Create the key with `setUserAuthenticationRequired(true)`; the `Cipher` you pass into the prompt only becomes usable after the system authenticates the user, so the crypto operation itself is the evidence.
• Only Class 3 (`BIOMETRIC_STRONG`) can gate a key. `BIOMETRIC_WEAK` cannot carry a `CryptoObject`, so a face-unlock-only device silently falls back — decide what happens there instead of discovering it in the field.
• Or in `DEVICE_CREDENTIAL` as the fallback. It is the only fallback that keeps out users with no usable biometric, and it is also the only way out of a permanent lockout.
• `setInvalidatedByBiometricEnrollment(true)` destroys the key when a new fingerprint is enrolled. `KeyPermanentlyInvalidatedException` is then a signal to re-authenticate with the real credential and re-wrap the token, not a crash.
• Call `canAuthenticate()` first — no hardware, none enrolled, and security-update-required each need different UI.

iOS:
• `LAContext.evaluatePolicy` is the boolean version and is acceptable only for a convenience gate over data you do not care about.
• For anything real, store the secret in the Keychain behind a `SecAccessControl` with `.biometryCurrentSet`, so reading the item is what triggers Face ID and no boolean sits on the path. `.userPresence` instead allows the passcode.
• `.biometryCurrentSet` invalidates the item when enrolment changes, which is the iOS equivalent of the Android behaviour above.

Things that get missed:
• Never store the user's password to replay it after a biometric prompt. Store a refresh token or a server-issued device secret, wrapped by the biometric-bound key.
• Repeated failures lock biometrics at the OS level, so the credential path is mandatory, not optional.
• Biometrics are shared and coercible. Keep a way to disable them, and keep step-up on the actions that move money.

question: Any app on the device can register your `myapp://` scheme. What breaks because of that, and what has to be true before you act on an inbound link?
answer:
A custom URL scheme is claimed on a first-come basis, so treat every inbound link as attacker-controlled input arriving at an endpoint anyone on the device can invoke.

Use links the OS can verify:
• Android App Links (`android:autoVerify="true"` plus `assetlinks.json`) and iOS Universal Links (the Associated Domains entitlement plus `apple-app-site-association`) are the only forms tied to a domain you proved you own.
• Verification happens at install time, so a malformed association file degrades silently to opening the browser. Test from a clean install and check the state with `adb shell pm get-app-links`.

Authentication in particular:
• Never carry an OAuth redirect on a plain custom scheme through the system browser — a competing app that registered the same scheme receives the authorization code. PKCE is what makes that stolen code useless, which is why it is mandatory rather than a nicety.
• Better still, use `ASWebAuthenticationSession` or Chrome Custom Tabs, which hand the result back to the app that started the flow, or an https App Link that cannot be claimed.

Treat the link as an unauthenticated request:
• Resolve it to a route, then re-check the session and the caller's right to that object on the server. A link that performs an action on arrival is the mobile shape of CSRF; anything destructive needs an explicit confirmation screen.
• Allow-list the host and the path, parse identifiers into typed values, and reject what does not match instead of matching loosely. A `next=` parameter you later navigate to, or load into a WebView, is an open redirect.
• Never put a token, a one-time code or PII in the URL. Links land in browser history, in server logs and in a referrer header when verification fails and a browser handles them instead.

Android's wider IPC surface comes attached:
• Declare `android:exported` on every component and keep it false unless something outside must reach it.
• Never pull an `Intent` out of an extra and start it. That is intent redirection, and it lets any caller reach your non-exported components with your app's permissions.
• `PendingIntent` must be created `FLAG_IMMUTABLE` unless you genuinely need the receiver to fill it in.

On iOS the equivalents are the `openURL` handler and `NSUserActivity` continuation. The calling application is not identified in any way you can trust, so never authorize on the basis of who appeared to send the link.

question: The device is already encrypted end to end. When does encrypting your own files actually add anything?
answer:
Full-disk encryption only protects a device that is powered off, so the real question is what an attacker holding your phone after one unlock, or holding your cloud backup, can still read.

What the platform gives you by default:
• iOS data protection is per file, and the default class is complete-until-first-user-authentication. After the user unlocks once following a boot, those files stay readable to anything running as your app — including an exploit running while the screen is locked. `.complete` makes the file unreadable whenever the device is locked, which also means your background task cannot touch it, so the class is a per-file decision.
• Android file-based encryption has the same shape. Credential-encrypted storage is the default and unlocks after the first unlock; device-protected storage is readable before any unlock at all, which is what direct-boot components use — so never put user data there.

What app-level encryption adds on top:
• A key that requires user authentication, which no first-unlock class gives you. A Keystore key with `setUserAuthenticationRequired`, or a Secure Enclave key behind `.biometryCurrentSet`, means the data is unreadable even to your own process until the user is present.
• A key you can destroy. Deleting the Keystore alias or the Keychain item makes gigabytes unreadable instantly, which is what makes logout and remote wipe real rather than best-effort.
• Encrypt the database with a passphrase held in the Keystore or Keychain, not one compiled into the app. SQLCipher or an encrypted Room or SQLDelight database is the usual route; remember the write-ahead log, the journal and any export or temp file inherit nothing from the main file's settings.

The backup surface is where forgotten data leaves the device:
• Android — `dataExtractionRules` controls cloud backup and device-to-device transfer separately, and `allowBackup="false"` alone is blunt and does not cover transfer.
• iOS — set the excluded-from-backup resource key on files, and use the `ThisDeviceOnly` Keychain accessibility classes so secrets stay out of iCloud and out of an encrypted local backup that could be restored onto another device.

Caches leak more than the database does. The URL cache writes response bodies to disk, image caches keep avatars, the app-switcher snapshot is a file on disk, and logs outlive the session. Put anything derived from user data in a directory you can delete, and make logout delete the database with its journal files, the caches, the temp directory and the key material. Keychain items in particular survive deleting the app on iOS.

question: Product wants to drop passwords and ship passkeys. What has to exist on your domain, on the server and in the app before that works?
answer:
A passkey is a public-key credential bound to your domain and held by the platform, so the app never handles a shared secret and a phishing site has nothing to collect.

The registration ceremony:
1. Your server issues a challenge and names the relying-party id, which is your domain.
2. The platform creates a key pair in secure hardware or the user's password manager, confirms with the user's biometric, and returns a signed response.
3. The server verifies the signature and the origin, then stores the public key and credential id against the account.

Sign-in is the same shape: server challenge, platform signature, server verification. Nothing secret crosses the wire in either direction.

Platform wiring:
• Android — Credential Manager, which puts passkeys, saved passwords and federated sign-in behind one system sheet. Your `assetlinks.json` must also carry the `get_login_creds` relation for your package name and signing certificate hash.
• iOS — the platform public-key credential provider from AuthenticationServices, with an Associated Domains entitlement declaring `webcredentials` for your domain. The autofill-assisted request is what makes the passkey appear above the keyboard rather than behind a button.
• Passkeys sync through iCloud Keychain or Google Password Manager, so a second device of the same ecosystem usually already has one. Crossing ecosystems uses the cross-device flow, where a QR code and Bluetooth proximity turn a phone into the authenticator for a laptop.

What teams get wrong:
• The relying-party id is a domain, so the association file is a hard prerequisite. An unpublished or malformed file produces an empty sheet, which looks exactly like an SDK bug and burns a day.
• You still need recovery and a fallback path. A user who loses their ecosystem account loses the credential, so keep a second factor, a second passkey or an email-based recovery.
• The biometric confirmation is local. Authentication is the server verifying the signed challenge, never the client reporting that the prompt succeeded.
• Credentials are per relying party, so a passkey cannot be used to correlate the user across sites.

question: Users keep turning up with a subscription they never paid for. Where does purchase validation usually go wrong?
answer:
Entitlement is a fact about an account on your server, and the classic bug is letting the app decide it from whatever the store SDK reported locally. A flag in preferences, or a receipt checked only in-process, is a boolean an attacker can write.

The division of labour: the client completes the purchase and hands the identifier to your backend. Whether it is active, whose it is, and whether it was refunded are all server questions.

Apple, with StoreKit 2:
• A transaction arrives as a signed JWS, and the verified case proves it came from Apple. It does not prove it belongs to this account or that it is still active, so the server checks the original transaction id against the App Store Server API.
• Subscribe to App Store Server Notifications V2 for renewal, refund, revocation and grace period. Those events happen while the app is not running, which is exactly when a client-side check cannot help.
• Set the app account token at purchase so the transaction is bound to your user id. Without it, a family or shared Apple ID hands the entitlement to whoever restores next.

Google, with Play Billing:
• The client receives a purchase token; the server verifies it through the Play Developer API and then acknowledges it. Failing to acknowledge within three days automatically refunds the user, which is the second most common bug in this area.
• Pass the obfuscated account id at launch so the purchase is bound to your user, and take the lifecycle from Real-time Developer Notifications on Pub/Sub rather than polling from the client.

Cross-cutting rules:
• Store the token or original transaction id uniquely and bind it to the first account that claimed it, so the same receipt replayed from a second account is rejected.
• Refunds and revocations must remove access, or buy-use-refund is a working exploit.
• Restore purchases has to be a real path — Apple requires it — and it must reconcile against the server rather than granting locally.
• Test in the sandbox, but never let a sandbox flag reach entitlement logic in the shipped build.
• Cache the server's verdict with an expiry so the app works offline, and choose the failure mode deliberately: fail closed for a new grant, fail open for a short window for someone whose subscription was already active.

question: The app calls a third-party API with the vendor key compiled into the binary. What do you replace it with?
answer:
Anything shipped inside a binary is public, so the fix is never a better hiding place but removing the client's need to hold the secret at all.

Why hiding fails: `strings` on the binary, an unzipped app bundle, or an interception proxy watching one request all recover the key in minutes. Splitting it across constants, moving it into native code, assembling it at runtime and stashing it in the Keystore are all a slightly longer afternoon for an attacker, and no more than that.

The default answer is to proxy the call. Your backend holds the vendor key, authenticates the user with your own session, rate limits per account, and logs the spend. The app talks only to your endpoint. Rotating the vendor key then costs a deploy rather than a store release, and a leak costs nothing.

When a key genuinely has to ship, because a maps or analytics SDK talks to the vendor directly:
• Restrict it at the vendor — bundle id on iOS, package name plus signing certificate hash on Android, an allow-list of which APIs it may call, a daily quota and a billing alert.
• A restricted key that leaks is an inconvenience. An unrestricted one is somebody else's compute bill.

Some values look like secrets and are not. A Firebase configuration file, a public SDK key, a crash-reporting DSN are all identifiers, and what protects the backend behind them is the server-side rule set plus App Check, which rejects clients that cannot produce a Play Integrity or App Attest token.

Prefer short-lived credentials to static ones wherever the vendor supports them: your server mints a token scoped to one user for a few minutes, optionally only after attestation succeeds.

Operational habits that matter as much as the design:
• Plan rotation before you need it. Know how to revoke, keep an overlap window, and treat any key that ever entered git history as burned — rewriting history does not un-clone the repository.
• Keep secrets out of source in the first place: CI secrets rather than a committed config file, a secret scanner as a pipeline gate, and push protection on the repository.
• Make a new SDK key a review question. Somebody has to answer what it can do if it leaks.
